extracted.intended_audience: criminal judges and trial practitioners (judges, magistrates, prosecutors, defence counsel) involved in taking testimony
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judges and trial practitioners on how to take, elicit, and evaluate witness testimony in criminal proceedings, including interpersonal techniques, cognitive precautions, and procedural habits. Focuses on preparing witnesses, managing testimony, assessing credibility, and avoiding investigator-driven distortions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: A judge must possess a knowledge of human nature acquired by persevering observation, comparison, and summarization rather than relying solely on books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text warns that rote memorization of manuals is of little use; practical, repeatedly-applied observational knowledge sets a practitioner ahead. Examples: horse-dealers, antiquarians, and card-sharps get by because they know people, not their trade. This human knowledge makes one independent of masses of factual information and is essential in assessing witnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive legal and scholarly knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge must be a jurist—not merely a criminalist—keeping fully up-to-date in theoretical and scholarly legal knowledge as well as practical acquaintance with many crafts and trades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neglecting theoretical study degenerates a judge into a mere laborer. The judge is ‘in duty bound’ to be familiar with diverse matters so he can form as much as possible from the legal material supplied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active elicitation of evidence (Integrity of witnesses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not simply throw a question to the witness and permit him to say what he chooses; the judge must do his best to bring out the uttermost value of the evidence, indifferently for or against the prisoner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaving full responsibility to a witness’s conscience is a dereliction. The judge must actively shape questioning and ‘educate’ the witness in the moment to get complete and accurate testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train witnesses to want and be able to tell the truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Training must make the witness both want to tell the truth (develop conscientiousness) and be able to tell the truth (capable of accurate recall and coherent reporting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first requirement concerns moral disposition (conscientiousness); the second concerns skills of perception and narration. Techniques differ: fostering conscientiousness vs improving ability to recollect and express facts. Target witnesses who habitually give 'approximately' rather than precise accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect and counter habitual approximations and loitering testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Be alert to people who give approximate, wandering, or retaliatory accounts rather than straight, prompt answers; these may do greater harm than obvious falsehoods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such witnesses often are not mistrusted and thus their insinuating approximations are dangerous. Recognize loitering conversational styles and apply methods (patience, setting starting points) to draw out the essential facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess credibility by social/occupational background
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain classes and occupations (peddlers, street merchants, inn-keepers, artists, prostitutes, congenital tramps) commonly provide less conscientious testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text offers this as one of the few exceptions/rules: 'the real tramps of both sexes and all walks of life will never testify conscientiously.' Use background as a heuristic in assessing likely reliability, while not treating it as absolute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and eliminate negative influences on observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Before relying on testimony, determine what conditions negatively affected a witness's observation or reproduction of events, decide which are operative, and aim to remove or allow for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative influences include fear, anger, prejudice, superstitions, or opinionative impressions. Distinguish essential observations from opinionative ones and try to substitute or isolate the former; this is often difficult and requires careful analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patience in taking testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise patience: allow witnesses who speak redundantly or prepared witnesses to tell their story rather than interrupting them prematurely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interrupting or shunting long-winded witnesses can cause loss of important material—prepared witnesses may bring out facts when allowed to run on. Use deliberate patience; if verbosity threatens, set specific start-points (e.g., 'Begin where X entered the room') to focus and preserve coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persist with laconic or monosyllabic witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: When witnesses answer only 'yes' or 'no,' apply prolonged, patient pursuit of consecutive answers to make their information coherent and usable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laconic witnesses may be unable to produce extended discourse; patient, sustained questioning can elicit enough to form a coherent narrative. Reading back statements may expose inaccuracies the witness does not notice otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine and meet the witness's level
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the witness's level of comprehension and experience and meet him on that level rather than presupposing he shares the questioner's frame of reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the Fröbelian maxim 'draw out, not probed.' You cannot raise a witness to your intellectual level in a few hours—work to match their apperceptive capacity and avoid overwhelming them with unfamiliar material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discover the witness's 'funded thought' (mental habits and concepts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Study a witness's habitual ways of thinking—their 'funded thought'—including vocabulary and conceptual frame, to avoid miscomprehension and mistaken inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a woodsman who lacks the concept of 'jealousy' gave testimony that was misinterpreted. Misunderstanding arises when interlocutors speak with different funded thoughts; uncover these to ensure you interpret answers correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presuppose as little as possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigidly avoid presupposing special knowledge, attention, or interest in witnesses; do not assume professional expertise or attention to detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excess material confuses witnesses; assuming they have observed or attended closely often leads to error. Even educated witnesses may be unreliable because their conscientiousness makes them doubt their perceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exemplification and analogy to aid recall
rubrics_metrics.description: Help witnesses recall and frame events by connecting new facts to similar experiences or familiar examples from their own life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring out a witness’s own analogous experiences to alter and improve their description (e.g., asking them to compare an event to a similar incident they personally experienced). This works with accused persons and juries as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor explanations and analogies to the jury's experience
rubrics_metrics.description: To make matters intelligible to jurors, connect new facts with instances familiar to them; find analogies for each event, motive, reaction or appearance so they can link them to known concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Difficult because a jury is composed of strangers; success when an analogy familiar to all jurors is found is especially valuable. Try to discover analogies for each important element of the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage egoism, laziness and conceit as motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Count on egoism, laziness and conceit as reliable human motives to encourage truthful, cooperative testimony; show personal interest and respect to engage witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People respond to personal interest—ask about their affairs, show comprehension of their trade, flatter appropriate pride. Avoid direct contradiction with obstinate individuals; provide face-saving means ('golden bridges') and indirect routes back to admission. The text asserts egoism is the most dependable human motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage secrets carefully (half-truths danger)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guard official secrets and be cautious about revealing partial facts; half-truths can be worse than whole lies because listeners will combine bare facts with other information to reach wrong conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not blab even seemingly harmless bare facts (anecdote: Boccaccio). Avoid dropping indications that allow extrapolation; remember that listeners synthesize bare facts with other knowledge, potentially ensnaring innocents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature disclosure of knowledge and unverified synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Never present the appearance of knowing more than you actually do; avoid asserting or revealing inferences as established facts because 'knowing something untrue' can mislead witnesses and derail inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judge's premature or over-confident presentation of synthesized possibilities can suggest facts to witnesses and corrupt evidence. Better to keep silence than to risk leading witnesses by demonstrating supposed knowledge based on unverified inference.
